content: NDUFB7, also referred to as NADH dehydrogenase 1 beta subcomplex subunit 7 or complex I-B18, is an enzyme encoded by the NDUFB7 gene in humans. This protein is an accessory subunit of the NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) complex, which is also known as Complex I. Complex I is the largest of the five complexes that constitute the electron transport chain and is located in the inner membrane of mitochondria. The NDUFB7 gene is situated on the short arm (p arm) of chromosome 19 at position 13.12. The gene spans approximately 6,000 base pairs in length. The NDUFB7 protein has a molecular weight of 16.4 kilodaltons and consists of 137 amino acids. It is a subunit of the NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) enzyme, which is the largest respiratory complex. Structurally, the protein adopts an L-shaped configuration. It contains a long, hydrophobic transmembrane domain and a hydrophilic domain that forms the peripheral arm. This peripheral arm houses all the known redox centers and the NADH binding site. Both NDUFB7 and NDUFB8 are localized at the intermembrane surface of Complex I. The N-terminal hydrophobic domain of NDUFB7 is capable of folding into an alpha helix that spans the inner mitochondrial membrane, while the C-terminal hydrophilic domain interacts with the globular subunits of Complex I. The two-domain structure of NDUFB7 is highly conserved, indicating its critical role in protein function. The hydrophobic domain serves as an anchor for the NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) complex within the inner mitochondrial membrane. The protein encoded by the NDUFB7 gene functions as an accessory subunit of the multisubunit enzyme NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, also known as Complex I. This subunit does not directly participate in the catalytic activity of the enzyme. Mammalian Complex I is composed of 45 distinct subunits and is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane. The protein complex exhibits NADH dehydrogenase and oxidoreductase activities, facilitating the transfer of electrons from NADH to the respiratory chain. Ubiquinone is believed to be the immediate electron acceptor for this enzyme. Alternative splicing of the NDUFB7 gene results in two transcript variants that encode distinct isoforms of the protein. The electron transfer process begins when NADH binds to Complex I, transferring two electrons to the isoalloxazine ring of the flavin mononucleotide (FMN) prosthetic group, forming FMNH2. These electrons are subsequently passed through a series of iron-sulfur (Fe-S) clusters within the prosthetic arm of the enzyme. Finally, the electrons are transferred to coenzyme Q10 (CoQ), reducing it to ubiquinol (CoQH2). The electron flow alters the redox state of the protein, inducing a conformational change and a shift in the pK of ionizable side chains. This process drives the pumping of four hydrogen ions (protons) out of the mitochondrial matrix, contributing to the generation of the proton gradient essential for ATP synthesis.
